questions.q: Why does a container image need its own scan, separate from Lesson 16's dependency scanning?
options: Because dependency scanning checks application dependencies, but not the base OS image's own packages
Because container images never contain application dependencies
Because image scanning and dependency scanning check exactly the same thing
Because Trivy only works on Kubernetes manifests
questions.explain: Dependency scanning covers packages declared in your application's manifest, but a container inherits a whole base OS image's packages too, which SCA never looks at — that's what image scanning covers.

questions.q: In the example Trivy scan output, what does the severity breakdown let a CI pipeline do?
options: Automatically patch every vulnerability without review
Gate the build on specific severities, such as blocking only CRITICAL findings with a fix available
Delete the vulnerable package from the internet
Ignore all findings regardless of severity
questions.explain: Breaking findings down by severity lets a team set a gate that blocks on the worst findings (like CRITICAL with a fix available) without failing every build over a low-priority issue.

A minimal base image containing only an application and its runtime dependencies, with no shell or package manager
An image that cannot be scanned for vulnerabilities
A deprecated image format no longer in use
questions.explain: Distroless images strip out the shell, package manager, and unnecessary OS packages, leaving far less attack surface and fewer packages that could carry a CVE.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a multi-stage Docker build?
options: To run the same build twice for redundancy
To compile in one stage and ship only the finished result in a separate, smaller final stage
To make builds slower but more secure
To avoid using a Dockerfile entirely
questions.explain: A multi-stage build keeps compilers, source code, and build tools in an earlier stage, copying only the finished artifact into a clean, minimal final image.

questions.q: Why does hardening matter even if a scan currently shows zero vulnerabilities?
options: Hardening is purely cosmetic and has no security benefit
A hardened image has fewer unnecessary packages, so the next disclosed vulnerability has less surface to land on
Hardened images are immune to all future vulnerabilities
Scanning becomes unnecessary once an image is hardened
questions.explain: Hardening reduces what's in the image in the first place, so even a currently clean scan benefits — fewer unnecessary packages means fewer places a future vulnerability can appear, and scanning still has to continue.
